A.explanation: A straight line with smaller constant gradient would mean constant smaller acceleration, but drag in air increases with $v$ so acceleration cannot stay constant.

B.explanation: This curve starts steeper than the vacuum line, implying initial acceleration greater than $g$, which is impossible when starting from rest where drag is zero.

C.explanation: Starting with gradient equal to $g$ then decreasing in gradient keeps $v$ below the vacuum line and shows acceleration falling toward zero as drag grows toward terminal velocity.

D.explanation: An increasing gradient means acceleration is increasing with time, whereas increasing drag must make resultant force and acceleration decrease.

hints: Notice the vacuum $v$ against $t$ graph is a straight line through the origin - its constant gradient is the acceleration $g$ with no air resistance.
Recall that in air the drag force starts at zero when $v=0$ and then increases as $v$ increases, so the resultant downward force $mg - \text{drag}$ gets smaller.
Compare the starting gradient and the way the gradient must change: which option starts with the same gradient as the vacuum line and then bends over with ever-decreasing gradient to stay below it?
walkthrough: In a vacuum the only force is weight, so acceleration is constant at $g$. On a $v$ against $t$ graph gradient equals acceleration, giving the straight line through the origin shown.

In air at $t=0$, $v=0$ so drag is zero. The resultant force is still $mg$ and initial acceleration is still $g$, so the air graph must start at the origin with the same initial gradient as the vacuum line.
As $v$ increases, drag increases upward. The resultant force $mg - \text{drag}$ decreases, so acceleration $a = (mg - \text{drag})/m$ decreases.

Decreasing acceleration means the $v$ against $t$ gradient must steadily decrease, giving a curve concave downwards that always lies below the vacuum line on the same scales and levels off toward terminal velocity.
Only the graph that starts with the vacuum gradient then bends over with falling gradient matches this cause-and-effect chain. This is option C.
